question: Producer refresh is 30 s and lag is 10 s. You want displayed TripUpdate data never older than the 90 s guideline under the simplified model. What is the longest poll interval that works?
explain: Worst-case age = L + R + poll = 10 + 30 + poll must be at most 90, so poll is at most 50 s. At 60 s the worst case is 100 s. The model ignores network time, so real systems leave some margin.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
question: A non-precise cache-miss profile puts most samples on an `add` that uses the value of the preceding load. What is the most likely reading?
options: The add instruction is unusually slow on this CPU
The profile is broken and should be discarded
Cache misses are caused by arithmetic instructions
The load is the real culprit; skid moved the recorded IP to a later instruction
explain: Skid means the IP is captured some instructions after the event. The add depends on the load, so it is where the stall shows up. Re-record with :pp to have PEBS or IBS attribute the samples to the load itself.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: A latency-critical service shows p99 spikes on allocation-heavy requests and a fast-rising compact_stall. THP is enabled=always, defrag=always. Which change targets the spikes while keeping most THP benefit?
options: Set defrag to defer so faults fall back to small pages and khugepaged collapses later
Set max_ptes_none to 0
Raise khugepaged pages_to_scan
Switch enabled to madvise and defrag to always
explain: The spikes come from direct compaction inside page faults. defer stops faults from stalling and leaves the work to kcompactd and khugepaged. max_ptes_none and pages_to_scan only affect khugepaged, not fault stalls, and madvise mode with defrag=always still stalls in any region the app marks.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
question: During decoding at 100K tokens of context, which part of a Mamba-2 layer's per-sequence memory grows with the context?
options: The SSM state h
The convolution buffer
Both, linearly in context length
Neither; both have fixed size
explain: Both the state (heads x head dim x N) and the convolution window (4 inputs) are fixed by the architecture. That fixed size is exactly why hybrids use these layers, and also why they cannot store unlimited exact detail.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
question: With k = 60, BM25 returns documents scoring 41.2 and 40.9 at ranks 1 and 2, and a second run with a different tokenizer returns 9.3 and 2.1 at ranks 1 and 2. How do the RRF contributions of these four positions compare?
options: The first run contributes far more because its scores are larger
Rank 1 gets 1/61 and rank 2 gets 1/62 in both runs; raw score gaps are ignored
The second run contributes more because its gap between ranks is bigger
They cannot be compared without normalizing first
explain: RRF uses only positions. That makes it immune to score scales (good) but blind to the fact that the second run is much more confident about its top hit (information lost). Bruch et al. argue this loss of score information is one reason a tuned convex combination can beat RRF.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search
question: Your corpus index was built with Contriever. A colleague proposes embedding the hypothetical documents with a different, stronger embedding model to save effort. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, any embedding model works with any index
Only latency increases
The LLM must then be retrained
The vector lands in a different embedding space, so inner products with the indexed Contriever vectors are meaningless
explain: HyDE relies on document-document similarity inside one space. The hypothetical passage must be encoded by the same encoder f that encoded the corpus, otherwise the averaged vector and the index vectors are not comparable.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
question: Why does a homography have 8 degrees of freedom rather than 9?
options: Because H and any nonzero multiple of H map every point to the same place
Because h9 is always 1 by definition
Because one equation per point is redundant
Because the bottom row must be (0, 0, 1)
explain: Scaling H scales X, Y and W together, and the division X/W, Y/W cancels it. So only 8 independent quantities matter. Setting h9 = 1 is a convention that fails when the true h9 is 0, and a fixed bottom row (0, 0, 1) would make H affine.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
question: Why does ECC alignment tolerate a change in exposure between the two images?
options: It compares zero-mean, normalized intensity vectors, so gain and offset cancel
It converts images to edges first
It uses RANSAC on pixel intensities
It only runs on binary masks
explain: The enhanced correlation coefficient subtracts each image's mean (removing an offset) and divides by its norm (removing a gain). Evangelidis and Psarakis point out that this makes the criterion invariant to brightness and contrast changes. It does not model local shadows.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
question: A configuration service does about 50 small reads per second in short bursts, on a 2-core VM that is already busy. A teammate proposes `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL` to save system calls. Good idea?
options: Yes, SQPOLL always lowers latency
Yes, but only with IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL as well
No: at 50 I/O per second the syscalls saved are negligible, and the poll thread competes for one of only 2 busy CPUs and keeps going to sleep between bursts
No, because SQPOLL requires root on all kernels
explain: SQPOLL pays off when a stream of submissions keeps the thread busy. Here it would mostly spin or sleep and wake, costing CPU on a constrained machine for almost no saved work. Privilege is no longer required on recent kernels, so that is not the reason.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
question: A latency-sensitive service shows p99 spikes every few seconds, and a profile shows time in page faults right after memory was purged. Which change targets this most directly?
options: Increase the number of size classes
Disable the thread cache
Lengthen the purge delay (jemalloc dirty_decay_ms or MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY) so freed pages stay mapped longer between bursts
Lower jemalloc's opt.narenas to 1
explain: The spikes come from returning pages to the OS and faulting them back in. A longer delay keeps them resident across bursts, at the cost of higher RSS. Disabling caches or arenas adds contention without fixing the faults.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: The nemesis: partitions, pauses, clocks and crashes
question: A coordination service hands out locks that expire if the holder misses heartbeats for 2 s. Which nemesis is most likely to show two clients holding the same lock?
options: Process pauses with SIGSTOP and SIGCONT lasting longer than the lease
A partition that isolates one follower that holds no locks
Bit flips in a log file on a single node
Packet duplication on a client link
explain: A paused holder cannot notice its lease expiring, so another client acquires the lock, and the first resumes believing it still holds it. Isolating an uninvolved follower or flipping bits does not target the lease mechanism.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Prune before you measure: shared memory and registers
question: A config that uses 144 KiB of shared memory tunes fine on a cc 9.0 GPU. The same tuning job runs on a cc 8.6 GPU and that config is now rejected. What should the tuner do?
options: Reduce num_stages automatically until it fits and keep the measured timing
Treat the limit as device state: prune against this device's limit and re-tune, because the legal space itself changed
Keep the cc 9.0 result, since the config is still correct code
Fail the tuning run, because the config list is invalid
explain: Shared memory per block is a documented per-capability quantity (227 KB at 9.0, 99 KB at 8.6), so the set of legal configurations is part of the device, not the kernel. Silently rewriting num_stages produces a config nobody measured, and carrying the old winner over is exactly the stale-cache failure of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
question: Why do DPDK and SPDK allocate I/O buffers from hugepages rather than plain malloc memory?
options: Because NICs cannot DMA into 4 KiB pages
Because VFIO only accepts 1 GiB pages
Because hugepages are faster for the device to read over PCIe
Because hugepages have physical addresses that Linux does not move today and are contiguous within a page, and they also cut TLB misses
explain: The device must be given addresses that stay valid. Hugepages are not migrated by Linux today and each one is physically contiguous; the TLB benefit is a bonus. With an IOMMU, VFIO pins and maps them explicitly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
question: A key-value service handles 50,000 requests per second per machine, shares cores with other services, and runs on laptops for development. Should it adopt DPDK?
options: Probably not: per-request kernel overhead is a tiny part of its budget, and bypass would burn dedicated cores, need root-level device setup and lose kernel tooling
Yes, bypass always lowers latency
Yes, but only with UIO to avoid needing an IOMMU
Yes, because hugepages alone will double its throughput
explain: At 50k requests per second each request has about 20 us of one core, so saving a microsecond of kernel path is noise. Bypass pays off near line rate, not for ordinary services.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
question: A fused kernel for a long row-wise reduction starts spilling registers and runs slower than two unfused kernels. Which fix matches what FlashAttention and Triton tutorials do?
options: Tile the reduction so each block of the row fits on chip, carrying running statistics between tiles
Fuse even more ops into the kernel
Switch to FP64 to get more registers
Disable the GPU's L2 cache
explain: Fusion is bounded by on-chip capacity. Tiling with running statistics (as in FlashAttention's online softmax) keeps the working set small while still avoiding HBM round trips for intermediates.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: tokens, sequences, on-policy
question: You can call a strong model only through a text API that returns completions, not probabilities. Which method can you still use?
options: Word-level distillation with soft targets
Sequence-level distillation: train the student with cross-entropy on the teacher's generated outputs
On-policy GKD with forward KL
Logit matching at high temperature
explain: Seq-KD only needs the teacher's output sequences. Word-level KD, logit matching and GKD all need the teacher's token-level probabilities (white-box access) on the relevant prefixes.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
question: A colleague quantizes both keys and values per-token at 2 bits and sees accuracy collapse, while 4-bit per-token worked fine. What is the most likely fix?
options: Use 3-bit per-token for both
Quantize values per-channel and keep keys per-token
Quantize keys per-channel and keep values per-token
Add more calibration data
explain: Per-token key groups get their range stretched by outlier channels, which wipes out the small channels at 2 bits. Per-channel keys fix that. In KIVI's Llama-2-13B test, keys per-token with values per-channel scored 2.80 on CoQA, worse than all per-token.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
question: Using the bars, which move gives the larger capacity gain over GQA-8 BF16: FP8, or keeping 20% of tokens in BF16?
options: FP8, about 2x
They are equal
20% kept, about 5x
Neither changes capacity
explain: FP8 halves bytes per token (59 to 119 sequences). Keeping 20% of tokens cuts per-sequence cache 5x (59 to 297), but with the risk of losing information permanently.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
question: A chatbot has 1,000 active sessions that each return every 5 minutes, and the host tier holds 600 sessions. Under strict LRU, what hit rate should you expect for returning sessions, and why?
options: About 60%, because the tier holds 60% of sessions
100%, because LRU keeps recently active sessions
About 50%, because LRU and FIFO behave the same here
Close to 0%, because each session is the least recently used by the time it returns, so it was just evicted
explain: With a cyclic access pattern larger than the cache, LRU evicts the oldest session, which is exactly the next one to return. Every return misses. Admission filtering that keeps a fixed subset resident, a bigger tier (SSD) or scheduler look-ahead all fix this; matching capacity alone does not.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
question: A node is at (10, 3). It performs a local event when its physical clock reads 11. What timestamp does the event get?
explain: l = max(10, 11) = 11, which differs from the old l, so c resets to 0: (11, 0). The reset is what keeps c bounded: as soon as the physical clock catches up with l, all accumulated ties are forgotten.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Inside the encoders: markers, [MASK] padding and training
question: A user types the 3-word query *who founded pixar*. With the default query length of 32, how many query vectors take part in MaxSim?
options: 3, one per word
4, one per WordPiece token
7, the tokens plus [CLS], [Q] and [SEP]
32, because the query is padded with [MASK] to 32 positions and every position yields a vector
explain: ColBERT pads every query to N_q = 32 with [MASK] tokens, and every position's output vector is used in MaxSim. So the query matrix is always 32 x 128, and the mask vectors act as learned expansion terms.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
question: In one step of ordinary CoT decoding, which operation discards the most information about the model's internal state?
options: The attention layers, because they average over earlier positions
Sampling a single token from softmax(W h), since only its identity is passed on
The final layer normalization before the LM head
The positional encoding added to the next input
explain: The next pass sees only e(x) for the one sampled token, a vector chosen from a fixed table of 50,257 rows. Everything else in the 768-dimensional h(t), including how probable the alternatives were, is dropped. Attention and normalization transform information but pass a full vector on.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
question: Adding 6 pause tokens vs. adding 6 Coconut thoughts to a 12-layer model: what happens to the longest serial chain of layer computations before the answer?
options: Both grow to 84 layers
Pause: stays 12. Coconut: grows to about 84
Pause: grows to 84. Coconut: stays 12
Both stay at 12 because attention is parallel
explain: A pause slot's input is a fixed embedding, so its computation happens in the same pass and every path climbs at most 12 layers. Each Coconut thought is the top-layer output of the previous pass fed in at the bottom, so 6 thoughts plus the final pass give 7 x 12 = 84.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
question: Why can uniform random keys need about as many segments as log-normal keys at epsilon 8?
options: The greedy algorithm is not optimal for uniform data
Uniform keys have duplicates
Linear models cannot represent a uniform CDF
At small scale, random gaps make the positions deviate from any line by more than 8 slots, so the distribution's global shape barely matters
explain: The uniform CDF is a straight line globally, but the actual positions of random keys wander around that line, and over 400,000 keys those excursions exceed 8 slots often. With a larger epsilon the wiggles fit inside the band and uniform data collapses to a single segment at eps 512. Model the data you have, not the distribution it came from.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
question: In doc-only mode, what work remains at query time?
options: Tokenizing the query and traversing the inverted index
Running the full transformer on the query
Re-encoding every candidate document
Nothing; results are precomputed per query
explain: The query is tokenized with the same vocabulary and each token gets a fixed weight (1 in SPLADE-doc, or a lookup table in OpenSearch). No transformer runs at query time.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
question: Two documents with different labels currently have identical scores. What is the RankNet cost of that pair (sigma = 1)?
options: 0, because the scores are not in the wrong order
ln 2, about 0.693, so the pair is still pushed apart
Infinite, because the probability is undefined
1, the maximum of the sigmoid
explain: At s_i = s_j the sigmoid gives P = 0.5 and C = ln(1 + e^0) = ln 2. Burges calls this a built-in margin: equal scores for differently labeled documents are still penalized.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
question: Why does regrouping $(QK^\top)V$ as $Q(K^\top V)$ fail for softmax attention?
options: Matrix multiplication is not associative
The softmax is applied to each row of $QK^\top$ before multiplying by V, so the product cannot be regrouped
Softmax attention uses different key and query dimensions
The causal mask makes regrouping impossible for any attention
explain: Associativity only holds for plain products. Softmax applies a nonlinear exp and normalization to every entry of $QK^\top$ first. Causal masking alone is fine: the running sum $S_t$ handles it.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise training and hybrid models in production
question: Qwen3-Next's context grows from 32K to 256K tokens. Which part of its per-sequence cache grows?
options: Only the KV cache of the 12 full-attention layers; the Gated DeltaNet state stays 72 MiB
Only the Gated DeltaNet state
Both grow 8x
Neither grows
explain: Gated DeltaNet layers keep a fixed $d_k\times d_v$ state per head regardless of length. The attention layers' KV cache grows linearly: 768 MiB at 32K to 6,144 MiB at 256K, while the 72 MiB state is unchanged.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
question: Your pairwise judge compares old ranker versus new ranker results and always shows the new ranker's result first. It reports a 58% win rate for the new ranker. What should you do first?
options: Ship the new ranker, 58% is a clear win
Rerun every comparison with the order swapped and count a win only when both orders agree; inconsistent pairs become ties
Switch to a longer prompt so the judge reads more carefully
Ask the judge to explain its reasoning and trust the explanation
explain: With a fixed order, position bias is confounded with the treatment. Swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) removes the position effect: wins must survive both orders. Randomising the order per pair is the cheaper large-scale alternative.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
question: Your new prompt makes answers about twice as long, and your LLM judge's pairwise win rate jumps from 50% to 68%. What is the best next step?
options: Ship it: 68% is a clear win
Check whether the gain survives at matched length, for example with a length-controlled regression or a human review of a sample
Switch the judge to single-answer grading, which has no length bias
Shorten the old answers by truncation and re-run
explain: Dubois et al. showed verbosity alone can move a win rate by tens of points. Estimate the preference at equal length (or ask people) before attributing the gain to quality. Single-answer grading is not immune to length bias, and truncation damages the baseline.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
question: You want to detect a 2-point change in pass rate, and the per-item difference has standard deviation about 0.4. Roughly how many items do you need for a 95% half-width of 0.02?
options: About 160
About 400
About 1,500
About 10,000
explain: n is about (1.96 x 0.4 / 0.02) squared = 39.2 squared, about 1,537 items. Small eval sets can only detect large changes.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Measuring a guard, and why no guard is complete
question: A guard has recall 0.9 and false positive rate 0.05. Harmful traffic is 0.5% of requests. Roughly what fraction of blocked requests are actually harmful?
options: About 8%
About 50%
About 90%
About 95%
explain: Precision = 0.9 x 0.005 / (0.9 x 0.005 + 0.05 x 0.995) = 0.0045 / 0.05425, about 0.083. With rare harm, even a 5% FPR means most blocks hit benign users.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
question: In the contiguous simulation, 12.8% of the pool was free yet the next request in line could not start. Which kind of waste is this?
options: Internal fragmentation
Reserved slots
Activation memory
External fragmentation
explain: Free memory existed, but not as one contiguous run long enough for the waiting request's reservation. That is external fragmentation. With fixed-size blocks any free block is usable, so external fragmentation disappears; the 0.5% left free in the paged run is just too few blocks for the next prompt.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
question: Your sentiment prompt has four examples, all labeled positive, and the model now labels most neutral reviews positive. What is the most likely cause?
options: Four examples are too few for in-context learning
The examples are not diverse, so the model picked up 'answer positive' as part of the pattern
Examples only affect format, never labels
The model needs gradient updates to learn labels
explain: Examples teach whatever pattern they share, intended or not. Anthropic's advice is to make examples diverse and to cover edge cases. Brown et al. show that examples steer behavior with no gradient updates at all.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
question: A summarization job uses a strict schema with max_tokens set to 200. About 3 percent of replies fail to parse even though constrained decoding is on. What is the most likely cause?
options: The decoder's mask has a bug that lets invalid tokens through
Those replies hit the 200-token limit and were cut off mid-JSON
The model refused, which always produces invalid JSON
JSON Schema cannot describe summaries
explain: A mask keeps every prefix valid and allows stopping only at an accept state, but the token limit cuts generation off regardless. Check the stop reason (max_tokens or incomplete) and raise the limit or shorten the output.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
question: Which cache key is safest for storing parsed filter objects?
options: The raw query string exactly as typed
The normalized query string alone
The normalized query plus the user's session ID
The normalized query plus the schema version and vocabulary version
explain: Raw strings fragment the cache on case and spacing. Without versions, a schema or dictionary change keeps serving stale parses (an old field name, a city ID that was split). The session ID would make the cache nearly useless, since the parse does not depend on who asked.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
question: At k=100, L=100, w=20, FIRST brings our modeled query latency from 10.35 s to 2.39 s. Which next change cuts FIRST's latency the most?
options: Raising the window step s while keeping w = 20, which removes windows and their prefill
Asking for a shorter permutation format
Using a higher sampling temperature
Adding a reasoning step before the ranking
explain: FIRST has no permutation to shorten, so the remaining time is prefill on a chain of windows. Fewer windows (or fewer tokens per window) is what is left. A reasoning step would add decode tokens back.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
question: Your API returns only generated text, no log-probabilities. Which pointwise method can you still run, and with what limitation?
options: Query likelihood, because it uses teacher forcing
Neither; pointwise prompts cannot work without fine-tuning
Yes/No generation, but you only get a binary label, so many passages tie and the ranking is coarse
Both, as long as you set temperature to 0
explain: Query likelihood needs the probability of the given query tokens, which a text-only API cannot provide. Yes/No still produces an answer, but without p(Yes) you only get two buckets, so passages inside a bucket keep their original order.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
question: Your listwise reranker works well on BM25 input but degrades badly when you switch the first stage to a new retriever that returns candidates in a near-random order. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Increase the window step so fewer windows are needed
Lower the temperature to 0
Shuffle the input several times and aggregate the rankings, or use a student trained with shuffled inputs
Switch to query likelihood, which is order-free but needs no changes
explain: The symptom is order sensitivity: failures and the one-pass guarantee both lean on a good initial order. Permutation self-consistency marginalizes the order out, and RankVicuna/RankZephyr train on shuffled inputs for the same reason. Temperature 0 makes outputs repeatable, not order-invariant.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Evaluating routers: cost-quality curves, PGR, APGR and CPT
question: A router has r = 7.6 on a benchmark where the weak model scores 6.5 and the strong model 8.4. What is its PGR?
explain: PGR = (7.6 - 6.5) / (8.4 - 6.5) = 1.1 / 1.9 = 0.579. 0.905 is 7.6 / 8.4, which ignores the weak baseline; 0.421 is 1 minus the right answer.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
question: You lower the ratio threshold from 0.8 to 0.6. What happens?
options: More matches survive and the outlier fraction rises
Nothing, since the ratio is scale-free
Every correct match is kept and only outliers are removed
Fewer matches survive and the surviving set has a lower outlier fraction
explain: A lower threshold demands a clearer winner, so fewer matches pass. Those that pass are less likely to be wrong, but some correct matches are lost too. Lowe's 0.8 removed 90% of false matches while losing under 5% of correct ones on the test data.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
question: A team uses 64-bit node indices plus a 16-bit tag packed into a 128-bit word and CASes it with a double-word CAS. Their threads can be descheduled for seconds. What is the honest risk statement?
options: ABA is impossible with any tag
ABA becomes very unlikely but not impossible: the 16-bit tag wraps after 65,536 successful CASes on that word
ABA is only possible on ARM
The tag makes the algorithm wait-free
explain: Michael and Scott: counters make ABA extremely unlikely but do not guarantee it never happens. At high CAS rates a 16-bit tag wraps in milliseconds, so a long stall gives many chances. With a 128-bit word there is room for a much wider tag, which is the cheap fix.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
question: Your service emits 50 GB of logs per hour and you must assign a template to every line as it arrives. Which property of a parser matters most for that?
options: It must achieve the highest possible accuracy on a labelled benchmark, whatever the cost
It must be online: constant work per line, no pass over the whole log before the first answer
It must store every raw line so templates can be recomputed later
It must know the number of distinct templates in advance to size its data structures
explain: At 33,000 to 56,000 lines per second you need bounded per-line work and no training pass. Offline parsers such as LKE are quadratic in the line count and could not finish four of five datasets in the Drain evaluation. Template counts are not knowable in advance, which is the whole problem, and retaining raw lines is a storage decision, not a parsing one.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
question: You cap Drain3 at max_clusters = 5000 with LRU eviction, and persist nothing. You restart the service. What breaks?
options: Nothing: the tree is rebuilt from the stream within a few seconds
Only the counts for templates that had been evicted before the restart
Parsing accuracy, because the LRU cache warms up in a different order
Every template id is reassigned from scratch, so every stored series, dashboard and trained model keyed on those ids silently refers to the wrong template
explain: Template ids are assigned by an incrementing counter as clusters are created. Without a persisted snapshot a restart renumbers everything in whatever order the stream happens to arrive, so id 7 now means something else. Drain3 exists partly to solve this: it snapshots state to a file, Redis or Kafka and reloads on startup. Accuracy itself recovers quickly; identity does not.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
question: A KV block arrives whose maximum score (5.0) exceeds the running maximum (3.0). What must the online softmax do with its existing denominator l and output o?
options: Multiply both by e^(3 - 5) before adding the new terms
Discard them and restart from the new block
Multiply only o by e^(5 - 3)
Nothing; maxima only matter for the final normalization
explain: Old terms were exponentiated relative to max 3. To express them relative to the new max 5, multiply by e^(3-5) = e^-2. Then add the new block's terms computed with max 5. Skipping this gives wrong weights.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
question: Which parameters does a Universal Transformer share across its recurrent steps?
options: Only the feed-forward transition; each step has its own attention
Only the attention; each step has its own transition
Both the self-attention and the transition function
Nothing; it shares weights across positions only, like any transformer
explain: In UT both the self-attention and transition weights are tied across steps, which is what makes the number of steps changeable. (Every transformer already shares weights across positions; that is not what makes UT recurrent.)

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
question: Aghajanyan et al. report d90 of about 200 for RoBERTa-Large on MRPC. What does this measure?
options: The number of training examples needed to reach 90% accuracy
The size of a random subspace in which training reaches 90% of full fine-tuning's score
The rank of RoBERTa-Large's weight matrices
The number of layers that must be fine-tuned
explain: d90 is the smallest dimension d of the trainable vector, projected randomly into the full parameter space, whose training reaches 90% of the full fine-tuning metric. It says nothing directly about data size or the rank of the pretrained weights.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
question: Which PEFT method from this lesson consumes part of the model's context window?
options: LoRA
(IA)3
DoRA
Prefix and prompt tuning
explain: Prompt and prefix tuning add virtual tokens that sit in the sequence, so they take positions that real input could have used. LoRA, DoRA and (IA)3 change weights or rescale activations and can be merged into the model.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff
question: Why does TOFU aggregate its nine utility numbers with a harmonic mean rather than an arithmetic mean?
options: It is faster to compute
So that one collapsed ability drags the score down instead of being averaged away
Because the metrics have different units
So that utility is always at least 0.5
explain: A harmonic mean is dominated by its smallest inputs. In the example, one score dropping to 0.02 moves the arithmetic mean only to 0.724 but the harmonic mean to 0.150. The TOFU authors chose it for exactly this reason: they did not want low scores to be averaged out.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
question: In a shortlist-then-rerank system with a Matryoshka model, recall@10 is too low. Shortlist K = 50 at D_s = 64, rerank at 1024. Which change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Rerank with 2048 dims instead of 1024
Store the full vectors in float64 for the rerank stage
Enlarge the shortlist (larger K) or use a larger D_s, so the right documents survive the first stage
Normalize only the query vectors
explain: Reranking can only reorder what the shortlist found. If relevant documents are cut in stage 1, a better stage 2 cannot bring them back. Raising K or D_s increases first-stage recall. Normalizing only the query does not change any order.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
question: Why does sequence parallelism not increase communication over plain TP?
options: It compresses activations before sending them
It skips the backward-pass communication
An all-reduce is a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather, and SP issues exactly those two halves at different points
It sends activations only between pipeline stages
explain: TP does 4 all-reduces per layer per step; TP + SP does 4 all-gathers and 4 reduce-scatters. A ring all-reduce is implemented as reduce-scatter then all-gather, so the bandwidth used is the same. The paper even measured a small speedup from running layer norm and dropout on 1/t of the data.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
question: A program allocates objects from 16 bytes to 128 KiB. A colleague says Robson's bound proves it will use 13x its live memory. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the bound applies to every program with that size range
Robson's bound only applies to garbage-collected languages
The bound is a worst case over adversarial sequences; real traces with good policies were near 0%
The bound is log base 10, so it is about 4x
explain: Robson's result says some request sequence can force that blow-up on any non-moving allocator. It does not say typical programs reach it. Johnstone and Wilson measured near-zero fragmentation for good policies on real programs.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
question: In `get_data`, someone changes the compare_exchange failure ordering from Acquire to Relaxed. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, because failure means no store happened, so ordering is irrelevant
The losing thread uses the winner's pointer without synchronizing with the Release that published it, so it may read uninitialized Data
The compare_exchange may now succeed twice
It only affects performance on x86
explain: On failure the operation still loads the winner's pointer, and that pointer is then dereferenced. Without Acquire on that load there is no happens-before from the winner's initialization, so the read of Data is a data race. Mara Bos uses Acquire for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
question: Which threads can possibly hold a reference to a node that was unlinked at time t?
options: Any thread that will run in the future
Only the thread that unlinked it
Only threads whose current operation started before t and is still running
No thread, because unlinking is atomic
explain: After the unlink, the node is unreachable from shared memory, so an operation starting later cannot find it. Only operations already in progress at time t may have loaded its address. Every scheme here is a way to detect when those operations have finished, or that they do not point at this node.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
question: A kernel subsystem keeps a routing table read millions of times per second and updated a few times per minute. Readers never sleep while holding entries. What is the best choice?
options: Hazard pointers on every table entry
A reader-writer lock
Reference counting each entry
RCU: readers use rcu_read_lock, updaters publish a copy and free with call_rcu or kfree_rcu
explain: This is RCU's design point: read-mostly data, non-sleeping readers and natural quiescent states. Readers make no shared writes, while hazard pointers would fence per visited entry and a reader-writer lock makes every reader write to the lock word. Rare updates make the grace-period wait cheap.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier
question: Why does ArcFace need the scale s at all?
options: To make the margin m measured in degrees
With unit vectors the logits are cosines in [-1, 1], so softmax can never become confident; s widens the logit range
To keep the class weights from growing
To normalize the features to unit length
explain: Cosines are bounded by 1. With s = 1 and 3 classes, even the best case (cosine 1 to the true class, -1 to the others) gives p = 0.787. Scaling by s lets the probabilities approach 1 so the cross-entropy can be driven down.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
question: Which setup best measures a function that in production runs once per request on cold data?
options: Many iterations on one small input with a long warm-up
Many iterations, each preceded (outside the timed region) by touching a buffer larger than the last-level cache, with batching to amortize pause overhead
One iteration, measured once
Many iterations on a single input with ASLR disabled
explain: Evicting the caches before each timed call recreates the cold state, and batching keeps the PauseTiming overhead small relative to the work. A long warm-up measures the hot case. A single run is dominated by noise and timer overhead. ASLR affects layout, not cache warmth.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
question: A harness re-serializes tool-call arguments (same JSON object, different whitespace) on every turn. Under the strict matcher, a linear session keeps rolling back. What is the narrowest fix the docs offer?
options: --session-message-matcher loose_tool_call
--session-message-matcher role_content_only
Pass --apply-chat-template so the harness renders the prompt
Set input_ids yourself in each request
explain: loose_tool_call accepts equivalent JSON-object argument representations while still requiring call IDs, function names and order to match. role_content_only would also work but can merge genuinely different tool histories. The docs say not to apply the chat template manually or set TITO control fields like input_ids.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives
question: A single-model learned index stores min error -3 and max error +2. What is the worst-case number of binary-search probes inside the window, compared with binary search over all 12 keys?
options: 1 probe versus 12
3 probes versus 4
6 probes versus 12
2 probes versus 3
explain: The window holds 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 slots. Binary search over n slots needs at most floor(log2 n) + 1 probes: 3 for 6 slots and 4 for 12. Probe counts scale with the log of the window, which is why shrinking error from thousands to tens matters more than shrinking it from 6 to 3.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
question: A model with 128 query heads switches from MHA to GQA with 8 groups, keeping $d_h$ and layer count fixed. By how much does its KV cache shrink?
options: 8x, because there are 8 groups
2x, because keys and values are both still stored
16x, because 128 key and value heads become 8
128x, because only one head is stored
explain: Cache is $2 n_g d_h l$ for GQA vs $2 n_h d_h l$ for MHA, so the ratio is $n_h / n_g = 128 / 8 = 16$. MQA would be the 128x case.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
question: You serve an MLA model on 8 GPUs and KV cache memory is the limit on batch size. Moving attention from 8-way tensor parallelism to 8-way data parallelism (each GPU holds all heads, different requests) mainly helps because:
options: Data parallelism makes the latent smaller
Under tensor parallelism each GPU keeps a full copy of every request's latent cache, so 8 GPUs hold 8 copies; under data parallelism each request's cache lives on one GPU
Tensor parallelism cannot run MLA at all
Data parallelism removes the need for the RoPE key
explain: The latent is shared by all heads, so splitting heads does not split the cache. vLLM documents this 8x duplication for DeepSeek-R1 at TP 8 and offers decode context parallelism as another way to avoid it.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
question: Using the simplified bandwidth model, which change most reduces the extra bytes read per step when 32 distinct adapters share each batch?
options: Raising the batch size to 64
Sorting rows by adapter
Using more prefill tokens per batch
Halving every adapter's rank
explain: Extra traffic is proportional to (distinct adapters) x rank. Halving the rank halves it. Sorting is required for SGMV to work but does not change how many adapter bytes must be read, and a bigger batch with more tenants can add distinct adapters.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
question: A LangChain `MultiQueryRetriever` with defaults is called through `invoke` over a base retriever with k = 5. What comes back?
options: The 5 highest RRF-scored documents
Up to 15 unique documents from the 3 rewrites, in the order they were retrieved
Exactly 20 documents including duplicates
Only the documents that appear in all 3 lists
explain: With include_original=False, 3 rewrites are searched (sequentially on the sync path) and the unique union is returned, up to 3 x 5 = 15 documents, in query order. There is no rank fusion and no truncation to k.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
question: Why does the pipeline run duoBERT on monoBERT's top 50 instead of directly on BM25's top 1000?
options: duoBERT cannot read passages that BM25 retrieved
Pairwise scoring grows as k(k-1): 1000 candidates would need 999,000 inferences instead of 2450
duoBERT is less accurate than monoBERT, so it should see fewer documents
BM25 scores must be normalized before a pairwise model can use them
explain: Pairwise cost is quadratic in the list length. On 1000 candidates, duoBERT would need 1000 x 999 = 999,000 inferences per query, about 290 times the 3450 that monoBERT plus duoBERT on 50 use. Putting the quadratic model last, on a short list, is exactly the cascade idea.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: Why does Margin-MSE train the student on score margins instead of making it reproduce the teacher's raw scores?
options: Different architectures naturally produce scores on different scales; only the ordering matters, and the margin preserves it
Raw scores are not available from cross-encoders
Margins are cheaper to compute at query time
MSE cannot be applied to raw scores
explain: A dot-product bi-encoder or ColBERT produces scores on a very different scale from a cross-encoder. Forcing the same raw values fights the architecture. Ranking only needs the student to separate relevant from non-relevant by the same amount, which is what the margin captures.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain
question: Why did the DeepSeek-V3 ablation conclude that MTP improved the model itself rather than just adding capacity?
options: The MTP models had more active parameters at inference
The module was discarded at inference, so the evaluated networks had identical cost and shape
MTP models were trained on more tokens
Only benchmarks that MTP helped were reported
explain: During evaluation the MTP module is dropped, so baseline and MTP models run the same main network at the same cost. The difference comes from how the shared weights were trained. The table even includes a regression (MMLU at large scale).

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: In SOAP, what happens if you force $Q_L = I$ and $Q_R = I$ for a layer?
options: The layer is trained with plain Adam
The layer is trained with Muon
The layer is frozen
The layer is trained with full-matrix AdaGrad
explain: With identity rotations, $G' = G$ and SOAP's inner step is an ordinary Adam step in the original coordinates. That is exactly what the paper does on very large sides such as the vocabulary dimension: it skips the rotation there because an $m \times m$ eigenbasis would be too costly.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
question: In the SP perceptron $f = V^\top U x$, which term in $f'$ is responsible for the blow-up after one step?
options: $V^\top U$, the initial output
$\theta\, V^\top V$
$\theta^2\, U^\top V$
$\theta\, U^\top U$
explain: $U$ has unit-variance entries, so $U^\top U$ is a sum of n squares of size 1, about n. $V^\top V$ is about 1 because V has variance 1/n, and the cross terms average out. The blow-up comes from the output layer's update $\theta U$, whose entries are order 1 while V was initialized at order $1/\sqrt{n}$. The input-side update $\theta V$ is tiny, which is the paper's point that SP's input layer learns too slowly.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
question: Why do good spin locks spin on a load before trying swap or CAS?
options: Loads are atomic and swaps are not
A load puts the thread to sleep in the kernel
A load keeps a shared read-only copy of the cache line, while each swap or CAS needs exclusive ownership of the line
Swap is not allowed while another thread holds the lock
explain: Every swap or CAS, even a failing one, needs the line in an exclusive state, so spinning with it bounces the line between cores. Loads let all spinners share a copy and stay quiet until the unlock store invalidates it.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
question: A real-time audio thread at high priority sometimes misses deadlines waiting on a mutex held by a low-priority logging thread, while medium-priority work is busy. What directly targets this?
options: Increase the mutex's spin count
Wake all waiters on every unlock
Use a priority-inheritance mutex, such as one built on PI futexes
Switch to FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG
explain: This is priority inversion. With priority inheritance the logging thread temporarily runs at the audio thread's priority while holding the lock, so the medium-priority work cannot starve it. More spinning only burns more CPU at high priority.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
question: In a dangerous structure T1 rw T2 rw T3, T3 has committed and T1 and T2 are still running. Which one does PostgreSQL prefer to abort, and why?
options: T1, because it started first
T2, because once retried it no longer overlaps the committed T3 and cannot form the same structure
T3, by rolling back its commit
None; it waits until all three commit
explain: Committed transactions cannot be undone. Aborting T1 would leave it concurrent with T2 on retry, so the same structure could reappear. Aborting T2 satisfies the safe retry property.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The metric: entity-level micro F1 with exact span match
question: Your model scores 91 micro F1 but 68 macro F1 on a five-type corpus. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Micro and macro were computed with different span-matching rules
One or two rare types are performing badly, and micro hides them because frequent types dominate the pooled counts
The model overfits the frequent types, which always lowers micro
Macro is always lower than micro, so the gap means nothing
explain: Micro pools counts, so the types with most entities set the number. Macro weights every type equally, so one weak rare type drags it down. Reporting both, with per-type support, is how you find the type that needs more data.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
question: Why does NSA insist on applying sparsity during pretraining instead of adding it to a finished dense model?
options: Sparse attention cannot run at inference time without training
Dense models have no attention sparsity to exploit
Post-hoc methods use more KV cache memory than NSA
Training with sparsity makes the model's attention patterns adapt to the selection, and it also makes long-context training itself cheaper
explain: A dense model's attention spreads mass in ways a fixed selector cannot fully capture (top 20% covers about 70% of mass in MagicPIG's measurements). Training natively lets the model learn patterns that fit the selector, and long-context pretraining and fine-tuning also get faster because the forward and backward passes are sparse.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
question: You want sparse attention for a model that will serve 1M-token contexts. Which statement is the best reading of the two designs?
options: NSA's decode speedup grows without limit, so it is strictly better
DSA needs no extra memory per token
Both remove the need to store the full KV cache
Both have a linearly growing per-query term (NSA's compressed tokens, DSA's indexer), so at extreme lengths the cheap scoring path becomes the bottleneck to optimize
explain: NSA reads about $s/d$ compressed tokens per step, capping its speedup near $d$. DSA's indexer scores all $L$ cached tokens. In both, the scoring or summarizing path scales with context, and both keep the full KV cache.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
question: A PDQ lookup returns a stored hash at distance 26 from the query, but the query's quality score is 20. What should the system do by default?
options: Report a confident match, since 26 is under 31
Recompute the hash at 128 bits
Treat the query hash as unreliable and not trust the match, since quality 49 or less is recommended for discarding
Rotate the image 90 degrees and try again
explain: Low quality means the image is nearly featureless (for example close to a solid color), and such hashes collide with many unrelated images. The PDQ README recommends discarding hashes with quality 49 or less, regardless of how close the distance looks.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
question: A multi-node Megatron run crashes on node 2 because it cannot find the converted checkpoint that node 1 created. What is the documented fix?
options: Set force_reconvert_from_hf: true on every step
Switch to the Automodel backend
Point NRL_MEGATRON_CHECKPOINT_DIR (or HF_HOME) at shared storage visible to all nodes
Lower gpu_memory_utilization
explain: The converted Megatron checkpoint directory must be accessible from all nodes, for example on NFS. The docs recommend a shared HF_HOME, which yields HF_HOME/nemo_rl.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
question: Thread A (node 0) and thread B (node 1) each write half of the same 4 KiB page first, at nearly the same moment. Where does the page live?
options: On whichever node's thread faulted first; the other thread's half is remote
Split: 2 KiB on each node
On both nodes, as a coherent copy per node
explain: A page is the smallest unit of placement. The first fault allocates the whole page on the faulting CPU's node, and the second thread then accesses it remotely. Give each thread page-aligned slices to avoid this.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
question: An API server's threads are spread over both nodes and the scheduler often moves them. Each request touches small, short-lived data. What is a reasonable default?
options: Pin every thread and bind all memory to node 0
Leave the default local policy, and consider automatic NUMA balancing rather than hand placement
Interleave all memory with numactl --interleave=all
explain: Short-lived per-request data is usually allocated and used by the same thread, so local allocation already places it well. Hard pinning removes scheduler flexibility, and binding to one node wastes the other controller. Hand tuning pays off for large, long-lived data.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
question: An NVMe I/O completion queue was created with 256 slots. What is the maximum number of completion entries it can hold before the controller must stop posting?
explain: The queue is full when head equals tail plus one, so one slot is always unused: 256 - 1 = 255. The spec says so explicitly: one slot in each queue is not available due to the head and tail pointer definition.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
question: A detector outputs two boxes on the same cat, both with IoU 0.9 against it. Under COCO matching, how are they scored?
options: Both are true positives
The higher-scoring one is a TP and the other is a FP
Both are false positives because the match is ambiguous
They are averaged into one detection
explain: Detections are matched in score order and each ground-truth box can be matched only once. The first takes the cat; the second has no unmatched ground truth left, so it is a false positive. This is why duplicates hurt AP.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
question: Why does SlateDB write each manifest version as a new numbered object (00...02.manifest, 00...03.manifest) instead of overwriting one manifest key?
options: S3 cannot overwrite objects
With create-if-absent on the next number, two writers cannot both install version N+1; a plain overwrite of one key is last writer wins
Numbered objects are cheaper to PUT
LIST is only consistent for new keys
explain: S3 can overwrite, and LIST is strongly consistent, but concurrent unconditional PUTs to one key resolve as last writer wins, silently losing an update. A conditional create on the next ID means exactly one of two racing writers succeeds, which is a compare-and-swap on the database state.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Cardinality: labels multiply, and a histogram multiplies again
question: Which single change cuts the series count the most for a histogram with 11 finite buckets and 24,000 label sets?
options: Halving the number of buckets
Replacing the histogram with a summary exposing three quantiles
Dropping the instance label, 50 values, by aggregating before storage
Shortening the metric name
explain: Dropping a 50-value label divides the series count by 50. Halving the buckets takes 14 series per label set down to 8, under a factor of 2, and destroys the resolution you need for percentiles. A three-quantile summary is 5 series per label set rather than 14, a factor of under 3, and it costs you the ability to aggregate at all. The metric name has no effect on series count.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
question: What does a CTC-trained recognizer need as training labels for each cropped line image?
options: A bounding box around every character
The frame index where each character starts
A segmentation mask of each glyph
Only the transcript string of the line
explain: CTC sums over all alignments that collapse to the transcript, so the model learns alignment on its own. This is the property CRNN highlights: train from images and label sequences with no character-level annotation.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build
question: A crash only happens in your Release build, and you need a debugger with line numbers but the same optimization level class. Which build type is the best first try?
options: Debug, since it has -g
RelWithDebInfo, which keeps optimization (-O2 for GCC) and adds -g
MinSizeRel, since it keeps NDEBUG
An empty CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE
explain: Debug drops optimization (only -g) and keeps asserts on, which can hide an optimizer-dependent or NDEBUG-dependent bug. RelWithDebInfo is optimized, defines NDEBUG like Release, and keeps debug info. It is still -O2 rather than Release's -O3, so the bug may move, but it is the closest standard type.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
question: A matrix has `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]`, `python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]` and one `exclude` entry for `os: windows-latest, python: "3.10"`. How many jobs does the matrix create?
explain: Product $2 \times 4 = 8$, minus the one excluded combination gives 7. Each is a separate job on a separate runner.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
question: A PR fixes a real bug and adds a test, but the reviewer would have named one helper function differently and prefers a slightly different loop style that the style guide does not mention. Under Google's standard, what should the reviewer do?
options: Request changes until both points are fixed, since the PR is not yet perfect
Approve, optionally leaving the naming and loop points as Nit: comments
Close the PR and write the fix themselves in their preferred style
Approve only after a third reviewer agrees on the naming
explain: The change definitely improves code health (a fixed bug plus a test). Style points not in the style guide are personal preference, so they should not block. Marking them Nit: keeps the feedback without delaying the merge.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge
question: Using the model with n = 2 and F = 2, a reviewer who used to take 8 hours per response now takes 4. How much does total time to merge drop?
options: From 28 h to 24 h
From 28 h to 16 h
From 28 h to 14 h
It does not change, since the author's work is the same
explain: Total is (n+1)R + nF. Before: 3 x 8 + 4 = 28 h. After: 3 x 4 + 4 = 16 h. Each hour saved per response is saved on all three rounds, so 4 hours faster per response saves 12 hours in total.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
question: Why does QEMU decline AI-generated patches even when the contributor fully understands and tests them?
options: Because AI code is always lower quality
Because the contributor cannot confidently certify the DCO when the copyright and license status of AI output is unsettled
Because it cannot be reviewed on a mailing list
Because QEMU forbids all tools, including static analysis
explain: QEMU's concern is provenance: the Signed-off-by line certifies the DCO, and with unclear licensing of AI output the project will not take the legal risk. It explicitly allows AI use for research, debugging and static analysis whose output is not in the patch.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
question: You rebase, your IDE silently runs `git fetch` every few minutes, and a maintainer pushed to your PR branch an hour ago. You run `git push --force-with-lease`. What happens?
options: It is rejected with stale info, because the maintainer's commit is newer than your rebase
It succeeds and overwrites the maintainer's commit, because the background fetch already updated your remote-tracking ref
It succeeds and keeps both, because a lease merges the histories
It is rejected because leases cannot be used on forks
explain: A bare lease compares the remote with your remote-tracking ref. The background fetch moved that ref to the maintainer's commit, so the lease matches and the forced update goes through. `--force-if-includes` would catch this, because the commit never appeared in your branch's reflog.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?
question: You want to copy an Apache-2.0 function into a Linux kernel driver (GPL-2.0-only). Which is correct?
options: Allowed, Apache-2.0 is permissive so it fits any project
Allowed, if you keep the NOTICE file
Not allowed as is: the FSF does not consider Apache-2.0 compatible with GPLv2
Allowed, because the kernel has a syscall exception
explain: Apache-2.0 is compatible with GPLv3 only. Its patent termination and indemnification terms are restrictions GPLv2 does not permit, so a GPL-2.0-only work cannot absorb it. The syscall exception concerns user programs calling the kernel, not code inside it.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
question: After `pyperf system tune` and CPU pinning, your runs vary by only 0.1%, and the patched build is 1.5% faster in every run. What can you still not conclude?
options: That the result is affected by noise
That the 1.5% comes from your change rather than a layout or order effect that favors the patched build
That the benchmark ran at all
That pyperf was installed correctly
explain: Low noise makes the gap statistically clear, but it says nothing about bias. Run order, code layout or environment size can shift one build consistently. Interleaving, rebuilding with different layouts or another machine tests for that.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Trace one request: a Redis GET from socket to reply
question: In a plugin-based web framework, `git grep -n -w handle_upload` finds only the definition and one line `routes = {"/upload": handle_upload}`. What is the best next search to find who runs it?
options: Conclude the function is dead code and propose deleting it
Search for `handle_upload(` with -w until a call appears
Search for where `routes` is read, for example `git grep -n -w routes`, to find the dispatcher that calls through the table
Search the tests for handle_upload
explain: A name stored in a table with no direct call is dynamic dispatch, as with Redis's command table. The caller looks up the table and calls the stored function, so search for the table's readers. Tests can help confirm behavior, but they do not show the production caller.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
question: Which repro is most likely to get a fast response on a library's issue tracker?
options: A link to a 2 GB dataset plus the 40-line script that loads it
A 3-row DataFrame built inline, the 6 lines that fail, and the full traceback
A screenshot of a notebook cell and its error output
Your entire notebook exported as a file
explain: Inline, artificial data plus a few failing lines and the full text traceback is copy-paste runnable. Downloads, screenshots and whole notebooks all push work onto the maintainer.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
question: Your PR moves `parser.c` into `lib/` and, while there, fixes an off-by-one in the moved function. What does the kernel guide recommend?
options: Keep both in one patch so the history shows the fix where the code now lives
Fix the bug first, then move the code in a second patch, or move first and fix second, but never modify code in the patch that moves it
Move the code and reformat it in the same patch, but put the fix separately
Leave the move out entirely; moves are never accepted
explain: The guide says not to modify moved code at all in the patch that moves it. That keeps the move verifiable as a pure move, and the fix shows up as a small, readable diff that history tools can track.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
question: Why does vLLM avoid a block size of 1 even though it minimizes wasted slots?
options: Block tables cannot store more than 1024 entries
Copy-on-write needs at least two tokens per block
Prefix caching only works with block sizes that are powers of two
The kernel processes fewer positions in parallel per fetch, underusing the GPU
explain: The paper explains that more tokens per block let the PagedAttention kernel process more positions in parallel. Too small underuses the GPU, too large raises internal fragmentation and lowers sharing. 16 was the default it chose.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
question: Why does stackcollapse-perf.pl strip offsets like +0x29 from each frame?
options: To make the output file smaller on disk
Because perf records the wrong offsets
Because flamegraph.pl cannot parse hexadecimal
So samples at different instructions in the same function merge into one stack line
explain: Two samples in convolve usually hit different instructions. With offsets kept they would be different stacks and the graph would split one function into many slivers. The script's header says offsets are stripped and identical stacks are coalesced with their counts summed.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
question: Which statement about the persistence domain on an ADR platform is correct?
options: Data is durable once the store instruction retires
Data is durable only once the 3D XPoint media has finished writing it
Data is durable once it reaches the memory controller's write pending queue
Data is durable once another core has read the new value
explain: ADR includes the WPQ: anything that reaches it is drained to the media on power failure. Retirement and visibility to other cores both happen while the line is still in a volatile cache. Waiting for the media itself is stronger than needed.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Alignment: which addresses a type is allowed to start at
question: On x86-64 Linux, which of these addresses is a legal start for a `double`?
options: 0x7ffc1018
0x7ffc1004
0x7ffc1012
0x7ffc100c
explain: A double has alignment 8, so the address must be a multiple of 8, meaning the low three bits are zero. 0x18 = 24 is a multiple of 8. 0x04 and 0x0c are only multiples of 4, and 0x12 = 18 is only even.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
question: You pass a Rust `struct Point { x: f32, y: f32, tag: u8 }` to a C function expecting `struct Point { float x; float y; uint8_t tag; }`. What must you add?
options: #[repr(C)]
Nothing, Rust always uses declaration order
#[repr(packed)]
#[repr(align(8))]
explain: Only #[repr(C)] guarantees the C algorithm: declaration order and C padding, giving the same 12 bytes. The default repr may reorder; packed would remove the tail padding C expects; align changes alignment but not order.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Scoring poses with Object Keypoint Similarity
question: Two models both miss every keypoint by 6 px on the same people. Model A's errors are on the face; model B's are on hips and knees. Which has higher OKS?
options: Model A, faces are small so errors matter less
They are equal, since distances are equal
Model B, because hips and knees have larger sigma so the same distance is penalized less
It depends only on the person's area
explain: With the same d and s, the similarity depends on kappa. Hip and knee sigmas (.107, .087) are three to four times the face sigmas (.025 to .035), so B keeps much higher similarities.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
question: Why does Lucene abandon the graph once it has visited more nodes than there are matching documents?
options: A flat scan costs one distance per match, a bound the walk has already exceeded, and it is exact
Lucene graphs cannot hold more nodes than the filter matches
Visiting too many nodes corrupts the HNSW index
The kNN filter is converted into a post_filter
explain: Brute force costs one distance per matching document. Once the walk has spent more distance computations than that, the graph is doing worse than a scan would, so Lucene switches to a plan with a known, bounded cost that is also exact.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Hardware prefetchers: patterns, training and the page wall
question: A loop reads two cache lines sequentially, then jumps to a random place and reads two lines again, and so on. Why does the hardware prefetcher help very little here?
options: Prefetchers only work on writes
The prefetcher requires 64 consecutive lines before starting
Random jumps disable the cache
After the two misses that train it, the stream ends, so its predictions point at lines that will never be read
explain: Training takes about two misses, and by then this short run is over. The prefetcher's guesses past the end become wasted bandwidth, the same overshoot Intel's manual warns about for short arrays.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Step labels without humans: Monte Carlo rollouts
question: You double the number of rollouts per step from 8 to 16 to 'make the labels more accurate', using hard estimation. Which error grows?
options: Correct steps labeled bad, because more rollouts mean more failures
Wrong steps labeled good, because more rollouts give a lucky recovery more chances to occur
Neither; HE labels converge to the truth as N grows
Both shrink equally
explain: HE marks a step good if any rollout succeeds. P(at least one recovery) = 1 - (1-r)^N rises with N, so wrong steps get marked good more often. Correct-step false negatives (1-q)^N fall. Math-Shepherd observed exactly this: larger N led to false positives.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
question: A thread in a 4-thread web server calls `chdir("/tmp")`, then another thread opens the relative path `log.txt`. Where does the file get opened?
options: In /tmp, because pthreads share CLONE_FS state such as the working directory
In the old working directory, because each thread keeps its own cwd
It depends on which CPU each thread runs on
The open fails because cwd changes are not allowed in multi-threaded programs
explain: pthread_create passes CLONE_FS, so the working directory is shared by all threads of the process. This is a real source of bugs: a library that calls chdir silently changes path resolution for every thread.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
question: Which workload benefits most from running more threads than cores?
options: Matrix multiplication that never blocks
A crawler where each request spends 95 percent of its time waiting on the network
A compression job reading from a RAM disk
A tight spin loop measuring time
explain: Threads that mostly wait free the core through voluntary switches, so extra threads overlap waiting with useful work. CPU-bound jobs gain nothing beyond the core count. (An event loop is the other way to get the same overlap with fewer threads.)

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Code size vs recall, and refinements: OPQ, fast scan, ScaNN
question: Your embeddings come from a model whose first 32 of 256 dimensions carry most of the variance. Plain PQ with M = 16 has poor recall. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase nprobe
Apply an OPQ rotation before PQ so variance is balanced across sub-spaces
Switch from ADC to SDC
Use k* = 16 instead of 256
explain: With the natural split, the first 2 sub-quantizers must represent most of the variance with 256 centroids each, while the rest waste bits. OPQ learns a rotation (for Gaussian data, Eigenvalue Allocation balances eigenvalue products) so each sub-space gets comparable energy. nprobe only matters for IVF list coverage.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
question: You run DSPy's BootstrapRS without passing a valset. It reports 0.92 on 50 training examples, and 0.81 on your test set. What most likely explains the gap?
options: The valset defaulted to the trainset, so demos were bootstrapped from and selected on the same examples
BootstrapRS always reports accuracy times 1.1
The test set must be mislabelled
Random search cannot overfit
explain: Per the DSPy docs the valset defaults to the trainset. The selected program contains demos drawn from those same examples and was chosen for scoring well on them, so its training score is optimistic. Pass a separate valset and keep a test set apart.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Noising frames: Gaussians on positions, IGSO(3) on orientations
question: Why does the rotation part of the forward process use IGSO(3) instead of adding Gaussian noise to the nine entries of R?
options: IGSO(3) is faster to sample than a Gaussian
Because a Gaussian perturbation of the nine entries leaves a matrix that is not orthonormal, so it is not a rotation at all
Because rotations have nine degrees of freedom and Gaussians only model three
Because the loss must be invariant to global rotation
explain: SO(3) is a curved manifold embedded in 9-dimensional space. Adding independent Gaussian noise to the entries leaves the manifold: columns stop being orthonormal and the determinant stops being 1. IGSO(3) is the transition density of Brownian motion that stays on the manifold.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
question: In the toy corpus, why did vehicle contribute 0.896 to d3 while car contributed only 0.666 to d1, both in 4-token documents?
options: vehicle appears in 1 document and car in 2, so vehicle has the higher IDF
Synonyms get an automatic 1.35x boost
d3 is shorter than d1
